items.stem: What is an exchange rate?
options: The price of one currency in terms of another
The rate of interest on foreign loans
The ratio of exports to imports
items.answer: The price of one currency in terms of another
items.markingKey: E.g. 1 euro = 1.10 US dollars.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a fixed and a floating exchange rate system.
items.answer: In a floating system the rate is set by market demand and supply with no target; in a fixed system the central bank pegs the rate to another currency and intervenes (reserves, interest rates) to keep it there.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: floating = market forces; 1 mark: fixed = peg maintained by intervention [2]

items.stem: Explain how a central bank can maintain a fixed exchange rate.
items.answer: It buys its own currency with reserves when there is excess supply and sells it when there is excess demand; it can also raise or lower interest rates to change capital flows.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: buying/selling with reserves; 1 mark: interest rates [2]

items.stem: The value of the kwacha is determined entirely by demand and supply in the foreign exchange market, with no central bank intervention. Which exchange rate system is being described?
items.answer: Floating exchange rate
items.markingKey: Floating exchange rate: market forces alone set the rate.

items.stem: The central bank of Calvania occasionally buys its currency to slow a rapid depreciation, without setting any official target. Which exchange rate system is being described? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Managed float: dirty float with intervention to smooth movements.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Managed float; 1 mark: explanation – dirty float with intervention to smooth movements. [2]

items.stem: Extract: The naira, which floats freely, fell from $1 = 15 naira to $1 = 18 naira over the year as investors moved money abroad following a cut in interest rates. Halvoria has a current account deficit of 5% of GDP and imports most of its fuel. Inflation has risen to 6% from 3%. Exporters of manufactured goods report rising orders, but the central bank is considering intervening to support the currency. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the value of the naira against the dollar. (b) Explain why inflation has risen.
items.answer: (a) 15/18 − 1 = −16.7%. (b) Import prices, especially fuel, rise in domestic currency (cost-push); higher export demand raises AD.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: 15/18 − 1 = −16.7%. [2] (b) Credit: Import prices, especially fuel, rise in domestic currency (cost-push); higher export demand raises AD. [2]

items.stem: Explain two disadvantages of a fixed exchange rate system.
items.answer: Large reserves needed; monetary policy must be used to defend the rate, not domestic goals; a deficit cannot be corrected automatically; speculative attacks; risk of an over- or under-valued rate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for two disadvantages, 1 mark each for explanation [4]

items.stem: In the foreign exchange market for the won, demand is Qd = 650 − 2P and supply is Qs = 500 + 4P, where P is the price of one won in US cents and Q is millions of won a day. The central bank of Valdoria fixes the exchange rate at 40 US cents per won. Calculate the excess supply of the currency at the fixed rate.
items.answer: 90 million won
items.markingKey: Qs = 660, Qd = 570; excess supply = 90 million.

items.stem: Which creates a demand for a country’s currency on the foreign exchange market?
options: Foreign residents buying the country’s exports
items.answer: Foreign residents buying the country’s exports
items.markingKey: They need the currency to pay.

items.stem: Explain how a floating exchange rate is determined.
items.answer: Demand for the currency comes from foreigners buying exports and assets; supply comes from residents buying imports and foreign assets; the equilibrium rate is where demand equals supply, and it changes when either shifts.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: sources of demand; 1 mark: sources of supply; 1 mark: equilibrium where D = S [3]

items.stem: Explain two factors that could cause a currency to appreciate.
items.answer: Higher relative interest rates (hot money); rising demand for exports; FDI inflows; lower relative inflation; speculation that it will rise; lower demand for imports.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for two factors, 1 mark each for explanation [4]

items.stem: The central bank of Halvoria raises interest rates while rates abroad are unchanged. What is the most likely effect on the market for the currency of Halvoria?
options: Demand for the currency rises; it appreciates
Demand for the currency falls; it depreciates
Supply of the currency falls; it appreciates
Supply of the currency rises; it depreciates
items.answer: Demand for the currency rises; it appreciates
items.markingKey: Demand for the currency rises; it appreciates: hot money flows in to earn higher returns.

items.stem: Households in Istrana buy many more imported smartphones. What is the most likely effect on the market for the currency of Istrana? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Supply of the currency rises; it depreciates: residents sell their currency to buy foreign currency for imports.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Supply of the currency rises; it depreciates; 1 mark: explanation – residents sell their currency to buy foreign currency for imports. [2]

items.stem: For each event, explain the effect on the demand for or supply of the currency of Umbria Nova and on its exchange rate. (i) The central bank of Umbria Nova raises interest rates while rates abroad are unchanged. (ii) Firms in Umbria Nova invest heavily in factories abroad.
items.answer: (i) Demand for the currency rises; it appreciates (ii) Supply of the currency rises; it depreciates
items.markingKey: (i) Demand for the currency rises; it appreciates – hot money flows in to earn higher returns. [2] (ii) Supply of the currency rises; it depreciates – outward investment requires selling the currency. [2] Total [4]

items.stem: Extract: The kip, which floats freely, fell from $1 = 8 kip to $1 = 10 kip over the year as investors moved money abroad following a cut in interest rates. Kestria has a current account deficit of 5% of GDP and imports most of its fuel. Inflation has risen to 6% from 3%. Exporters of manufactured goods report rising orders, but the central bank is considering intervening to support the currency. (a) State whether this is a depreciation or a devaluation, and explain why. (b) Explain why inflation has risen.
items.answer: (a) Depreciation: a fall in a floating rate driven by market forces. (b) Import prices, especially fuel, rise in domestic currency (cost-push); higher export demand raises AD.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Depreciation: a fall in a floating rate driven by market forces. [2] (b) Credit: Import prices, especially fuel, rise in domestic currency (cost-push); higher export demand raises AD. [2]

items.stem: Extract: The rupiah, which floats freely, fell from $1 = 12 rupiah to $1 = 15 rupiah over the year as investors moved money abroad following a cut in interest rates. Tarvia has a current account deficit of 5% of GDP and imports most of its fuel. Inflation has risen to 8% from 5%. Exporters of manufactured goods report rising orders, but the central bank is considering intervening to support the currency. (a) Explain why inflation has risen. (b) Explain why the current account may not improve immediately.
items.answer: (a) Import prices, especially fuel, rise in domestic currency (cost-push); higher export demand raises AD. (b) J-curve: demand is price inelastic in the short run; Marshall–Lerner may not be met yet.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Import prices, especially fuel, rise in domestic currency (cost-push); higher export demand raises AD. [2] (b) Credit: J-curve: demand is price inelastic in the short run; Marshall–Lerner may not be met yet. [3]

items.stem: Which creates a supply of a country’s currency on the foreign exchange market?
options: Foreign firms investing in the country
items.answer: Domestic residents buying imports
items.markingKey: They sell domestic currency for foreign currency.

items.stem: Extract: The yuan, which floats freely, fell from $1 = 12 yuan to $1 = 15 yuan over the year as investors moved money abroad following a cut in interest rates. Valdoria has a current account deficit of 4% of GDP and imports most of its fuel. Inflation has risen to 6% from 3%. Exporters of manufactured goods report rising orders, but the central bank is considering intervening to support the currency. (a) Using a demand and supply diagram, explain how the cut in interest rates caused the fall. (b) Explain why inflation has risen.
items.answer: (a) Lower returns lead to capital outflows: supply of the currency rises (and demand falls), lowering the equilibrium rate. (b) Import prices, especially fuel, rise in domestic currency (cost-push); higher export demand raises AD.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Lower returns lead to capital outflows: supply of the currency rises (and demand falls), lowering the equilibrium rate. [4] (b) Credit: Import prices, especially fuel, rise in domestic currency (cost-push); higher export demand raises AD. [2]

items.stem: What is a depreciation of a currency?
options: A fall in the rate of inflation
A fall in its value decided by the government in a fixed system
A fall in its value in a floating exchange rate system
items.answer: A fall in its value in a floating exchange rate system
items.markingKey: Market-driven fall.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a depreciation and a devaluation.
items.answer: Both are falls in a currency’s value; a depreciation is caused by market forces in a floating system, while a devaluation is an official decision to lower a fixed rate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: depreciation market forces/floating; 1 mark: devaluation official/fixed [2]

items.stem: Explain why an appreciation of one currency against another means a depreciation of the other.
items.answer: An exchange rate is a ratio: if one unit of A buys more of B, then one unit of B buys less of A, so B has fallen in value against A.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: exchange rate is relative price; 1 mark: rise in one is fall in other [2]

items.stem: Under its fixed exchange rate system, Korvia officially lowers the value of the yuan by 20% to restore competitiveness. Which term best describes this change?
items.answer: Devaluation
items.markingKey: Devaluation: deliberate official reduction in a fixed rate.

items.stem: Under its fixed exchange rate system, Fendaria officially lowers the value of the kip by 20% to restore competitiveness. Which term best describes this change? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Devaluation: deliberate official reduction in a fixed rate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Devaluation; 1 mark: explanation – deliberate official reduction in a fixed rate. [2]

items.stem: Extract: The kwacha, which floats freely, fell from $1 = 8 kwacha to $1 = 10 kwacha over the year as investors moved money abroad following a cut in interest rates. Lunaria has a current account deficit of 6% of GDP and imports most of its fuel. Inflation has risen to 8% from 5%. Exporters of manufactured goods report rising orders, but the central bank is considering intervening to support the currency. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the value of the kwacha against the dollar. (b) Explain why the current account may not improve immediately.
items.answer: (a) 8/10 − 1 = −20%. (b) J-curve: demand is price inelastic in the short run; Marshall–Lerner may not be met yet.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: 8/10 − 1 = −20%. [2] (b) Credit: J-curve: demand is price inelastic in the short run; Marshall–Lerner may not be met yet. [3]

items.stem: Speculators sell the floating naira and its value against the dollar falls by 12%. Which term best describes this change?
items.answer: Depreciation
items.markingKey: Depreciation: market-driven fall in a floating currency.

items.stem: A depreciation of a country’s currency is most likely to
options: reduce the price of imported raw materials
make its exports cheaper in foreign currency and its imports dearer in domestic currency
make its exports dearer and imports cheaper
items.answer: make its exports cheaper in foreign currency and its imports dearer in domestic currency
items.markingKey: Price competitiveness improves.

items.stem: Explain the Marshall–Lerner condition.
items.answer: A depreciation improves the current account only if the sum of the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports exceeds one; then the rise in export volumes and fall in import volumes outweigh the lower price received for exports and higher price paid for imports.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: PEDx + PEDm > 1; 1 mark: volume effects outweigh price effects [2]

items.stem: Explain the J-curve effect of a depreciation.
items.answer: In the short run demand is price inelastic (contracts, habits), so import spending rises and export revenue rises little: the current account worsens. Over time volumes respond, the Marshall–Lerner condition is met and the current account improves.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: short run inelastic, worsens; 1 mark: long run elastic, improves [2]

items.stem: Six months after a depreciation, Nordavia’s current account deficit has widened before beginning to narrow. Which effect of the exchange rate change is shown?
options: Higher net exports and economic growth
items.answer: J-curve effect
items.markingKey: J-curve effect: demand is price inelastic in the short run.

items.stem: Six months after a depreciation, Istrana’s current account deficit has widened before beginning to narrow. Which effect of the exchange rate change is shown? Explain your answer.
items.answer: J-curve effect: demand is price inelastic in the short run.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: J-curve effect; 1 mark: explanation – demand is price inelastic in the short run. [2]

items.stem: For each case, identify the effect of the exchange rate change on the economy and explain it. (i) The won appreciates by 18% and exporters of solar panels in Korvia lay off workers. (ii) Six months after a depreciation, Korvia’s current account deficit has widened before beginning to narrow.
items.answer: (i) Higher unemployment in export industries (ii) J-curve effect
items.markingKey: (i) Higher unemployment in export industries – exports become dearer and demand falls. [2] (ii) J-curve effect – demand is price inelastic in the short run. [2] Total [4]

items.stem: Extract: The rand, which floats freely, fell from $1 = 8 rand to $1 = 9.6 rand over the year as investors moved money abroad following a cut in interest rates. Nordavia has a current account deficit of 4% of GDP and imports most of its fuel. Inflation has risen to 6% from 3%. Exporters of manufactured goods report rising orders, but the central bank is considering intervening to support the currency. (a) State whether this is a depreciation or a devaluation, and explain why. (b) Explain why inflation has risen.
items.answer: (a) Depreciation: a fall in a floating rate driven by market forces. (b) Import prices, especially fuel, rise in domestic currency (cost-push); higher export demand raises AD.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Depreciation: a fall in a floating rate driven by market forces. [2] (b) Credit: Import prices, especially fuel, rise in domestic currency (cost-push); higher export demand raises AD. [2]

items.stem: Extract: The kwacha, which floats freely, fell from $1 = 10 kwacha to $1 = 12.5 kwacha over the year as investors moved money abroad following a cut in interest rates. Calvania has a current account deficit of 4% of GDP and imports most of its fuel. Inflation has risen to 8% from 5%. Exporters of manufactured goods report rising orders, but the central bank is considering intervening to support the currency. (a) Explain why inflation has risen. (b) Explain why the current account may not improve immediately.
items.answer: (a) Import prices, especially fuel, rise in domestic currency (cost-push); higher export demand raises AD. (b) J-curve: demand is price inelastic in the short run; Marshall–Lerner may not be met yet.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Import prices, especially fuel, rise in domestic currency (cost-push); higher export demand raises AD. [2] (b) Credit: J-curve: demand is price inelastic in the short run; Marshall–Lerner may not be met yet. [3]

items.stem: Explain how an appreciation can affect inflation, growth and employment.
items.answer: Import prices fall and export demand falls: lower inflation (cheaper imports, weaker AD), but lower net exports reduce AD, growth and employment in export industries.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: inflation falls; 1 mark: net exports fall; 1 mark: growth/employment fall [3]

items.stem: Explain why the effect of a depreciation on firms depends on how much they import.
items.answer: Exporters gain competitiveness, but firms that import raw materials or components face higher costs, which can offset the price advantage.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: export competitiveness; 1 mark: higher imported input costs [2]

items.stem: In a floating exchange rate system, the exchange rate is determined by
options: the demand for and supply of the currency on the foreign exchange market
the central bank setting an official rate
items.answer: the demand for and supply of the currency on the foreign exchange market
items.markingKey: No official target.

items.stem: Explain why a government might choose a managed float rather than a pure float.
items.answer: It gains the flexibility of market rates but can intervene to reduce excessive volatility and speculation, giving traders more certainty.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: flexibility; 1 mark: reduces volatility/certainty [2]

items.stem: Sundara links its currency to the euro at a fixed rate and holds large euro reserves to defend it. Which exchange rate system is being described?
items.answer: Fixed exchange rate
items.markingKey: Fixed exchange rate: a peg against an anchor currency.

items.stem: Esteria has kept its currency pegged to the US dollar for ten years. Explain the differences between floating, fixed and managed exchange rate systems.
items.answer: Floating: market D and S; fixed: peg defended by reserves and interest rates; managed: float with intervention; diagrams of intervention.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Floating: market D and S; fixed: peg defended by reserves and interest rates; managed: float with intervention; diagrams of intervention. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: A rise in a country’s interest rates relative to other countries will most likely
options: increase supply of its currency and cause it to depreciate
have no effect on the exchange rate
increase demand for its currency and cause it to appreciate
items.answer: increase demand for its currency and cause it to appreciate
items.markingKey: Hot money inflows.

items.stem: Explain how speculation can affect a floating exchange rate.
items.answer: If speculators expect the currency to rise they buy it, raising demand and causing the rise they expected; expectations of a fall lead to selling and depreciation; this can increase volatility.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: buying/selling on expectations; 1 mark: self-fulfilling/volatility [2]

items.stem: Lina makes the following statement: ‘A floating exchange rate is determined by the government’s budget.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: It is determined by demand for and supply of the currency, from trade, investment, interest rate and speculative flows.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – It is determined by demand for and supply of the currency, from trade, investment, interest rate and speculative flows. [2]

items.stem: The market for the baht is described by Qd = 640 − 3P and Qs = 80 + 4P, where P is the price of one baht in US cents and Q is millions of baht traded a day. Calculate the equilibrium exchange rate.
items.answer: 80 US cents

items.stem: The market for the rupiah is described by Qd = 800 − 5P and Qs = 440 + 4P, where P is the price of one rupiah in US cents and Q is millions of rupiah traded a day. (a) Calculate the equilibrium exchange rate and quantity. (b) Foreign demand for Quentara’s exports rises, increasing demand for the rupiah by 18 million a day at every exchange rate. Calculate the new equilibrium exchange rate and quantity.
items.answer: (a) 9P = 360: P = 40 US cents, Q = 600 million. (b) New Qd = 818 − 5P: P = 42 US cents, Q = 608 million; the rupiah appreciates by 5%.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) new rate [1]; quantity [1] [4]

items.stem: (a) Explain, using a diagram, how a floating exchange rate is determined and why it might change. (b) ‘Changes in interest rates are the most important influence on the exchange rate of Lunaria.’ Discuss this statement.
items.answer: (a) Demand from exports, inward investment and hot money; supply from imports and outward investment; equilibrium; shifts from interest rates, inflation, incomes, speculation. (b) For: Hot money flows are large and fast; central banks use interest rates to influence currency. Against: Trade flows, relative inflation, FDI, speculation and confidence also matter; long-run rates follow competitiveness; judgement. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement on when the claim holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Indicative content: Demand from exports, inward investment and hot money; supply from imports and outward investment; equilibrium; shifts from interest rates, inflation, incomes, speculation. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8] (b) Analysis (AO1/AO2, up to 8): Hot money flows are large and fast; central banks use interest rates to influence currency. Evaluation (AO3, up to 4): Trade flows, relative inflation, FDI, speculation and confidence also matter; long-run rates follow competitiveness; judgement. Top marks need balanced analysis of both sides and a justified conclusion that answers the question set, explaining what the outcome depends on [12]

items.stem: What is a devaluation?
options: A rise in a fixed exchange rate
A market-driven fall in a floating rate
A fall in the price level
An official reduction in the value of a fixed exchange rate
items.answer: An official reduction in the value of a fixed exchange rate
items.markingKey: Government/central bank decision.

items.stem: Explain why a government might devalue its currency.
items.answer: To make exports cheaper and imports dearer, improving competitiveness and the current account, or because it can no longer defend the peg with reserves.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: competitiveness/current account; 1 mark: unable to defend peg [2]

items.stem: The exchange rate between the won and the US dollar changes from $1 = 20 won to $1 = 24 won. By what percentage has the value of the won in US dollars changed?
Explain the difference between a depreciation and a devaluation, and why a government might devalue its currency.
items.answer: Depreciation market-driven in floating system; devaluation official in fixed system; reasons: competitiveness, current account, unsustainable peg.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Depreciation market-driven in floating system; devaluation official in fixed system; reasons: competitiveness, current account, unsustainable peg. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: In a revision note Hana wrote: ‘A depreciation will always improve the current account of Sundara.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: It improves only if the Marshall–Lerner condition holds; in the short run (J-curve) it may worsen the current account.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – It improves only if the Marshall–Lerner condition holds; in the short run (J-curve) it may worsen the current account. [2]

items.stem: Leila makes the following statement: ‘An appreciation of the naira will make Pelora’s exports cheaper abroad.’ Explain what is wrong with this claim.
items.answer: An appreciation raises the foreign-currency price of exports, making them less competitive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – An appreciation raises the foreign-currency price of exports, making them less competitive. [2]

items.stem: An exporter in Umbria Nova sells laptops for 1200 kwacha per unit. The exchange rate changes from $1 = 8 kwacha to $1 = 7.2 kwacha. Calculate the new US dollar price of each unit, assuming the exporter keeps its price in kwacha unchanged.

Estimates for Ostrelia: the price elasticity of demand for exports is −0.4 in the short run and −0.8 in the long run; for imports it is −0.3 in the short run and −0.5 in the long run. Imports make up 30% of the consumer price index. The currency depreciates by 20%. What is the likely effect on the current account?
options: It worsens in both the short run and the long run
It improves in both the short run and the long run
It improves in the short run and worsens in the long run
It worsens in the short run and improves in the long run
items.answer: It worsens in the short run and improves in the long run
items.markingKey: Short run sum 0.7 < 1 (worsens); long run sum 1.3 > 1 (Marshall–Lerner met, improves): J-curve.

items.stem: An exporter in Calvania sells cement for 600 rupiah per unit. The exchange rate changes from $1 = 8 rupiah to $1 = 7.2 rupiah. (a) Calculate the US dollar price before and after the change, and the percentage change. (b) Explain the likely effect on the quantity exported.
items.answer: (a) Before: 600/8 = $75; after: 600/7.2 = $83.33; change +11.1%. (b) The dollar price rises, so the quantity demanded abroad tends to fall; the size depends on price elasticity of demand.
items.markingKey: (a) both prices [1]; % change [1] (b) [1] [3]

items.stem: Extract: The won, which floats freely, fell from $1 = 12 won to $1 = 14.4 won over the year as investors moved money abroad following a cut in interest rates. Marvona has a current account deficit of 6% of GDP and imports most of its fuel. Inflation has risen to 6% from 3%. Exporters of manufactured goods report rising orders, but the central bank is considering intervening to support the currency. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the value of the won against the dollar. (b) Using a demand and supply diagram, explain how the cut in interest rates caused the fall.
items.answer: (a) 12/14.4 − 1 = −16.7%. (b) Lower returns lead to capital outflows: supply of the currency rises (and demand falls), lowering the equilibrium rate.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: 12/14.4 − 1 = −16.7%. [2] (b) Credit: Lower returns lead to capital outflows: supply of the currency rises (and demand falls), lowering the equilibrium rate. [4]

items.stem: What must a central bank do to maintain a fixed exchange rate when there is excess supply of its currency?
options: Buy its own currency using foreign currency reserves
items.answer: Buy its own currency using foreign currency reserves
items.markingKey: Increases demand to restore the peg.

items.stem: Kenji wrote in a homework answer: ‘Under a fixed exchange rate system, Lunaria does not need foreign currency reserves.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: Reserves are essential to buy the currency when there is excess supply and so defend the peg.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Reserves are essential to buy the currency when there is excess supply and so defend the peg. [2]

items.stem: In the foreign exchange market for the naira, demand is Qd = 500 − 5P and supply is Qs = 140 + 4P, where P is the price of one naira in US cents and Q is millions of naira a day. The central bank of Lunaria fixes the exchange rate at 50 US cents per naira. Calculate the excess supply of the currency at the fixed rate.
items.answer: 90 million naira
items.markingKey: Qs = 340, Qd = 250; excess supply = 90 million.

items.stem: Extract: The baht, which floats freely, fell from $1 = 10 baht to $1 = 12 baht over the year as investors moved money abroad following a cut in interest rates. Merania has a current account deficit of 4% of GDP and imports most of its fuel. Inflation has risen to 8% from 5%. Exporters of manufactured goods report rising orders, but the central bank is considering intervening to support the currency. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the value of the baht against the dollar. (b) State whether this is a depreciation or a devaluation, and explain why. (c) Using a demand and supply diagram, explain how the cut in interest rates caused the fall.
items.answer: (a) 10/12 − 1 = −16.7%. (b) Depreciation: a fall in a floating rate driven by market forces. (c) Lower returns lead to capital outflows: supply of the currency rises (and demand falls), lowering the equilibrium rate.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: 10/12 − 1 = −16.7%. [2] (b) Credit: Depreciation: a fall in a floating rate driven by market forces. [2] (c) Credit: Lower returns lead to capital outflows: supply of the currency rises (and demand falls), lowering the equilibrium rate. [4]

items.stem: Why does the demand curve for a currency slope downwards?
options: Speculators always buy when the rate falls
A lower exchange rate makes imports cheaper
A lower exchange rate makes the country’s exports cheaper, so more currency is demanded to buy them
Interest rates rise as the currency falls
items.answer: A lower exchange rate makes the country’s exports cheaper, so more currency is demanded to buy them
items.markingKey: Derived demand.

items.stem: In a revision note Mei wrote: ‘A floating exchange rate is determined by the government’s budget.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: It is determined by demand for and supply of the currency, from trade, investment, interest rate and speculative flows.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – It is determined by demand for and supply of the currency, from trade, investment, interest rate and speculative flows. [2]

items.stem: Explain, using a demand and supply diagram, what happens to the value of the rand when foreign tourists visit Korvia in greater numbers.
items.answer: Tourists buy the rand to spend in Korvia, so demand for the rand shifts right; the equilibrium exchange rate rises (appreciation) and quantity traded increases.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: demand shifts right; 1 mark: exchange rate rises [2]

items.stem: Households in Valdoria buy many more imported solar panels. What is the most likely effect on the market for the currency of Valdoria?
options: Supply of the currency falls; it appreciates
Demand for the currency falls; it depreciates
Demand for the currency rises; it appreciates
Supply of the currency rises; it depreciates
items.answer: Supply of the currency rises; it depreciates
items.markingKey: Supply of the currency rises; it depreciates: residents sell their currency to buy foreign currency for imports.

items.stem: The market for the baht is described by Qd = 900 − 5P and Qs = 240 + 6P, where P is the price of one baht in US cents and Q is millions of baht traded a day. (a) Calculate the equilibrium exchange rate and quantity. (b) Foreign demand for Esteria’s exports rises, increasing demand for the baht by 44 million a day at every exchange rate. Calculate the new equilibrium exchange rate and quantity.
items.answer: (a) 11P = 660: P = 60 US cents, Q = 600 million. (b) New Qd = 944 − 5P: P = 64 US cents, Q = 624 million; the baht appreciates by 6.7%.

items.stem: Extract: The rupiah, which floats freely, fell from $1 = 10 rupiah to $1 = 12 rupiah over the year as investors moved money abroad following a cut in interest rates. Jovania has a current account deficit of 5% of GDP and imports most of its fuel. Inflation has risen to 7% from 4%. Exporters of manufactured goods report rising orders, but the central bank is considering intervening to support the currency. (a) State whether this is a depreciation or a devaluation, and explain why. (b) Using a demand and supply diagram, explain how the cut in interest rates caused the fall. (c) Explain why inflation has risen. (d) Explain why the current account may not improve immediately. (e) Discuss whether the central bank should intervene to support the currency.
items.answer: (a) Depreciation: a fall in a floating rate driven by market forces. (b) Lower returns lead to capital outflows: supply of the currency rises (and demand falls), lowering the equilibrium rate. (c) Import prices, especially fuel, rise in domestic currency (cost-push); higher export demand raises AD. (d) J-curve: demand is price inelastic in the short run; Marshall–Lerner may not be met yet. (e) For: limit imported inflation, reduce uncertainty, prevent capital flight. Against: uses reserves or higher interest rates that slow growth; depreciation helps exporters and the deficit; depends on inflation target and size of fall; judgement.

items.stem: The exchange rate changes from $1 = 10 pesos to $1 = 12 pesos. What has happened?
options: There has been no change in value
The peso has appreciated against the dollar
The peso has depreciated against the dollar
The dollar has depreciated against the peso
items.answer: The peso has depreciated against the dollar
items.markingKey: More pesos per dollar: each peso is worth less.

items.stem: In a revision note Arjun wrote: ‘The exchange rate moved from $1 = 20 won to $1 = 25 won, so the won appreciated.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: More won are needed to buy one dollar, so each won is worth less: the won has depreciated.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – More won are needed to buy one dollar, so each won is worth less: the won has depreciated. [2]

items.stem: The central bank of Lunaria announces that its fixed rate will change from 2 to 2.5 naira per US dollar. Which term best describes this change?
items.answer: Devaluation
items.markingKey: Devaluation: an official reduction in a fixed rate (more naira per dollar).

items.stem: Price elasticity of demand for Fendaria’s exports is −0.3 and for its imports is −0.4. Explain the likely effect of a depreciation on its current account.
items.answer: The sum of the elasticities is 0.7, less than 1, so the Marshall–Lerner condition is not met; the current account is likely to worsen.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: sum 0.7 < 1; 1 mark: current account worsens [2]

items.stem: Six months after a depreciation, Lunaria’s current account deficit has widened before beginning to narrow. Which effect of the exchange rate change is shown?
options: Higher net exports and economic growth
items.answer: J-curve effect
items.markingKey: J-curve effect: demand is price inelastic in the short run.

items.stem: An exporter in Sundara sells furniture for 1200 kip per unit. The exchange rate changes from $1 = 3 kip to $1 = 4.5 kip. Calculate the new US dollar price of each unit, assuming the exporter keeps its price in kip unchanged.

An exporter in Ostrelia sells laptops for 2400 won per unit. The exchange rate changes from $1 = 3 won to $1 = 3.6 won. (a) Calculate the US dollar price before and after the change, and the percentage change. (b) Explain the likely effect on the quantity exported.
items.answer: (a) Before: 2400/3 = $800; after: 2400/3.6 = $666.67; change −16.7%. (b) The dollar price falls, so the quantity demanded abroad tends to rise; the size depends on price elasticity of demand.
items.markingKey: (a) both prices [1]; % change [1] (b) [1] [3]
